trials.prompt: a heroic knight with a sword and shield
trials.notes: bayer dithers the flat background into checkerboard noise and makes the sprite harder to read; undithered is cleaner. Both weak overall: the flux source is a good sprite but occupies ~40% of canvas, so 32x32 downscale starves it — auto-crop-to-subject before downscale is the real fix (next axis to test).

trials.prompt: a heroic knight with a sword and shield
trials.notes: zimage's source fills the frame (~70% subject coverage) vs flux's ~40%, so the 32x32 downscale keeps a fully readable knight (helmet/sword/shield legible, good silhouette). flux side is an unreadable blob at this scale. Residual: background speckle from zimage source noise survives cleanup — auto-crop and background handling are the next axes.

trials.prompt: a heroic knight with a sword and shield
trials.notes: With a clean modern source (zimage), 'standard' preprocessing amplifies fine noise into background speckles that survive quantization; the raw source quantizes much cleaner (near-uniform background, same silhouette readability). Direct confirmation of Next-Phase §2's over-processing hypothesis: good models need less correction.

trials.prompt: a heroic knight with a sword and shield
trials.notes: Near-identical: modern pixel-art-styled sources (zimage) already draw their own dark outlines, so the auto-outline pass is a visual no-op; keep it on as a harmless default for sources that lack outlines.

trials.prompt: a heroic knight with a sword and shield
trials.notes: No-op: zimage's scattered background speckles count as subject pixels, inflating the naive bbox to the full frame so autoCrop bails. Needs a noise-robust bbox (percentile-of-subject-mass trim) — retest after. On clean-background sources (flux) offline reprocessing shows autoCrop is a dramatic win.

trials.prompt: a heroic knight with a sword and shield
trials.notes: Percentile-mass bbox fixed the speckle no-op: autoCrop now crops through the noise and the knight fills the 32x32 frame — shield emblem legible, clean silhouette, background speckles cropped away. Biggest single quality lever found so far; strong candidate for recipe default on single sprites.

At 16x16 the crop is existential: without it the small-in-frame flux subject downscales to two unreadable smudges; with autoCrop the robot has a readable silhouette, limbs, and shading. autoCrop matters more the smaller the target scale.

trials.prompt: a heroic knight with a sword and shield
trials.notes: Without the orphan-cleanup pass, stray single blue/orange pixels survive around the sprite (helmet, sword base, right edge); with cleanup the same frame is speckle-free and otherwise identical. Cleanup stays on.

trials.prompt: a feral alchemist with a grappling hook, inspired by Kid Icarus
trials.notes: K-Centroid vs mode downscale on a zimage source at ideal nes settings: near-identical silhouette and palette; B (k-centroid) has a slightly muddier/softer transition at the right shoulder-to-background boundary where A (mode) keeps a crisper edge, but the difference is marginal and wouldn't affect shippability either way. Need more trials before this axis moves the ideal.

trials.prompt: a cybernetic goo dragon, inspired by Pokémon Red
trials.notes: At 16x16, mode downscale (A) drops almost all subject detail -- the frame is nearly blank background with a few scattered stray pixels, unreadable as a dragon. K-Centroid (B) recovers substantially more structure (a body outline, a horizontal tail/arm bar, an eye dot) because it clusters each tile's colors instead of taking a strict per-pixel mode, so minority-but-substantial subject-color clusters within a tile survive instead of losing to background on a technicality. Neither is a great sprite, but B is meaningfully more readable. First decisive win for k-centroid — worth another trial or two on gameboy before promoting.

trials.prompt: a boss monster made of living crystal, inspired by Wario Land
trials.notes: Second gameboy downscale trial, different prompt/seed, explicit mode-vs-k-centroid champion reset (earlier auto-picked champion had silently inherited k-centroid from the prior verdict -- watch for this when re-testing an axis that already won). A (mode) is a readable but flat monochrome silhouette. B (k-centroid) keeps the same silhouette and edge cleanliness but uses more of the 4-shade Game Boy palette (a mid-tone shading patch, a distinct dark eye pixel) instead of collapsing near-tied tile colors to a single flat green -- better hardware-palette utilization at no readability cost. Second decisive win for k-centroid on gameboy; promoting gameboy-tiny's recipe.
